correctness.limitations: The finite census compares with the values in the frozen record; it does not certify the publisher's table or the asymptotic argument. Only odd composites are counted, not primes, even integers, or the class of integers having just one carry-free factorization. No sharp exponent is claimed.
correctness.rationale: Every eligible odd composite supplies an odd nontrivial factor pair with injective one-bit sums, so counting even the larger set of all such pairs is an upper bound. Assign highest bit indices t≤B and k=t+B≤floor(log₂ X). If t≤B/2, the mandatory bits 0 and t in a forbid two bits of b at distance t. The graph of that restriction on 0,…,B is a disjoint union of t paths. Matching within each path gives at least (B+1−t)/2≥B/4 disjoint edges, so at most 2^(B+1)(3/4)^(B/4) strings survive. Multiplying by at most 2^t candidates for a and using B≥2k/3 gives O(2^(ϑk)) with ϑ=1−log₂(4/3)/6. If t>B/2, B<2k/3, and injectivity into the k+1 positions implies that one factor has weight at most √(k+1). This costs only 2^O(√k log(k+2)) choices for that factor, while the other has at most 2^(B+1) choices. The resulting exponent is below ϑk for large k; finitely many small cases are absorbed with an absolute constant. There are at most k+1 splits for each k, and the sum grows geometrically up to a linear factor in floor(log₂ X). The bound and the density conclusion follow without the finite counts.
